newsitem.title: USA: US 30-yr repo rate dives to 1 pct as demand soars.
newsitem.headline: US 30-yr repo rate dives to 1 pct as demand soars.

text.p: U.S. 30-year bonds seemed to be the trade of the day in the U.S. Treasury maket on Friday, rocketing ahead of short and intermediates, analysts said.
Need evidence? Look no further than the repo market, where overnight financing for the bond had sunk to around 1.0 percent during Friday morning trading after opening at 3.0 percent.

"(Bonds) are in heavy demand due to renewed positive sentiment that we will continue to have a Golidlocks economy: no inflation smoking gun and no demand pressures," said Kevin Flanagan, money market eocnomist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

Market participants also said foreign accounts were gobbling up bonds quickly. With the shorter end of the curve seen as having reached the limit of its rally, the long end was the place to be, they added.
"Two-years had been special but it is garbage now trading at 5.25 percent," said a repo trader at a primary dealership.
Tom Pearl, managing director of the repo desk at Chase Securities Inc, went on to say that "with more demand out the curve, it makes sense (long end repo rates) are tighter."
On Monday, 30-year overnight repo rates traded as high as 5.40 percent, not all that much lower than the 5.68-5.73 percent general collateral rate.

Since then, 30-year repo rates have steadily fallen, trading down to around 3.0 percent on Thursday and threatening to break below 1.0 percent on Friday. General collateral, meanwhile, was around 5.40 percent on Friday morning.
"This is a chance in the repo market to make some money," said the trader at the primary dealership.
He said the drop in repo rates was a relief to the market, which had been financing bond positions at rates of up to 100 basis points of negative carry in the last few weeks.

The bullish sentiment enticed retail buying. Traders noted that a number of firms had reallocated asset models into bonds. Plus, the numerous corporate and global issues led to swapping and hedging at the longer end.
With high demand for bonds, dealers were willing to lend money at low levels. Some even predicted that bond repo rates could drop further to approach zero percent in late Friday trading.

"There are sizable shorts in the cash market," said a repo trader. "We have rallied so much that the market has not priced in a tightening at all ... So, we have repo players buying bonds all the way to August 15."
Wall Street specialists said, however, the party may not last that much longer.
"It is probably going to stay tight for a few days into next week," the trader said.
"(But) this is as hot as it is going to get," he added.

Analysts said yields on the 30-year maturities -- which are around 6.65 percent, a four-month low -- already reflect recent evidence that the economy is slowing and that the Federal Reserve may keep rates steady in July.
They added the market was not likely to move ahead any further unless some fresh evidence of an continuing economic slowdown emerges.
For many weeks, the 10-year note and sometimes the five-year were the hot issues in the repo market.

The 10-year, which has benefitted from the Treasury's decision to eliminate two 10-year auctions, still trades tight at around 4.0 percent. The five-year, however, has backed off and trades at nearly 5.0 percent.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
